becoming-a-discerning-consumer-of-food.d: Becoming a Discerning Consumer of Food
terms: Food labelling
The legally required information on packaging, including ingredients, allergens, weight and dates, that helps consumers make informed choices.
Marketing and advertising
Techniques such as packaging design, special offers and branding that influence consumer decisions, which discerning shoppers learn to assess critically.
Nutritional information panel
The per-100g and per-portion table on packaging showing energy, fat, saturates, sugars and salt so products can be compared.
Traffic-light labelling
A front-of-pack scheme using red, amber and green to show at a glance whether a food is high, medium or low in fat, sugars and salt.
Use-by and best-before dates
Date marks indicating food safety (use-by) and quality (best-before), helping consumers avoid both risk and waste.
Value for money
Comparing the price, quantity and quality of products, for example using unit pricing, to judge which option offers the best deal.

being-an-effective-consumer-of-food.d: Being an Effective Consumer of Food
terms: Budgeting
Planning shopping around a set amount of money, comparing prices and avoiding waste to make food spending go further.
Consumer rights
The legal protections shoppers have, such as the right to refunds for faulty or misdescribed food under consumer protection law.
Food labelling
The mandatory packaging information, including ingredients, allergens and date marks, that enables consumers to choose safely and wisely.
Informed choice
Selecting food based on accurate information such as labels, prices and nutritional content rather than on advertising alone.
Special offers
Promotions such as buy-one-get-one-free or multibuys that can save money but may also encourage over-buying and food waste.
Unit pricing
Showing the price per standard measure, such as per 100g or per litre, so consumers can compare products of different sizes fairly.
Carbohydrates
Energy macronutrient; simple (sugars) and complex (starch, fibre); 4 kcal/g.
Energy balance
Energy in (food) versus energy out (BMR + activity); imbalance leads to weight change.
Fat
Concentrated energy (9 kcal/g); saturated (animal) and unsaturated (plant); essential fatty acids.
Fibre
Indigestible plant material aiding gut health; adults need ~30 g/day.
Protein
Built from 20 amino acids; needed for growth and repair; 4 kcal/g.
Water
Essential for hydration, temperature regulation and transport; ~2 L/day recommended.
Additives
Substances added to food to preserve it or improve its colour, flavour or texture, such as preservatives, emulsifiers and antioxidants.
Food preservation
Methods such as freezing, canning, drying and pickling that extend shelf life by slowing or preventing microbial growth and spoilage.
Mass production
Making large quantities of a standardised food product on a production line to a consistent specification at a lower cost per item.
Pasteurisation
A heat treatment that destroys harmful bacteria in liquids such as milk by heating briefly to a set temperature then rapidly cooling.
Primary processing
The first stage of converting a raw food into a usable form, such as milling wheat into flour or pasteurising milk.
Secondary processing
Turning processed ingredients into food products, such as baking flour into bread or making milk into cheese and yoghurt.
Caramelisation
The browning of sugars when heated to high temperatures, which adds colour and a sweet, rich flavour to foods such as onions.
Coagulation
The setting of protein when heated, for example egg white turning solid, important in cooking eggs, meat and baked goods.
Cooking methods
Techniques such as boiling, steaming, roasting, grilling and frying, each chosen to suit particular foods and the result required.
Dovetailing
Planning the order of tasks so that several dishes are prepared efficiently and are ready at the same time when cooking a meal.
Gelatinisation
The thickening process in which starch grains absorb liquid and swell when heated, used to thicken sauces such as a roux-based sauce.
Heat transfer
The movement of heat into food by conduction, convection and radiation, which underlies how all cooking methods work.
Fairtrade
A certification ensuring producers in developing countries receive a fair, guaranteed price and better working conditions for their goods.
Food miles
The distance food travels from where it is produced to where it is eaten, often used as an indicator of its environmental impact.
Food provenance
Information about where food was grown, reared or caught and how it was produced, which informs consumers about its origin.
Food security
Having reliable access to enough safe, affordable and nutritious food, a concern affected by climate, trade and population growth.
Organic food
Food produced without most artificial pesticides and fertilisers and with higher animal-welfare standards, certified to defined organic rules.
Seasonality
Eating foods at the time of year they are naturally harvested locally, which can cut cost and environmental impact and improve flavour.

food-safety-food-science-and-special-die.d: Food Safety, Food Science and Special Diets
terms: Diabetic diet
Manages blood glucose; emphasises low-GI carbohydrates, portion control.
Gluten-free
Excludes wheat, barley, rye; essential for coeliac disease.
Halal
Islamic dietary rules; meat from animals slaughtered with prayer; no pork or alcohol.
Kosher
Jewish dietary rules from Torah; no pork, shellfish; meat and dairy kept apart.
Vegan
Excludes all animal products; needs vitamin B12 supplementation.
Vegetarian
Excludes meat and fish; lacto-ovo includes dairy and eggs.
